## formal
Let $J(v) = v \cdot B$ with $B = e_{1}e_{2} + e_{3}e_{4} + \dots + e_{2n+1}e_{2n+2}$ on $\R^{2n+2}$, the quarter turn in every coordinate plane, $G = \langle g \rangle \cong \Z_{4}$ acting on the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}$ by $g = J$, and $\Sig_{n} = L^{2n+1}(4) = S^{2n+1}/G$. Let $\eta$ be the flat oriented plane bundle on which $g$ acts by the quarter turn, $\eta^{2}$ the one on which it acts by the half turn, and $\shL$ the flat real line on which $g$ acts by $-1$, so that $\shL \oplus \shL = \eta^{2}$. Background (G), general and classical, not derived here: cellular chains of a regular cell structure compute singular (co)homology; for a free cellular action the cochains of the quotient are the invariant cochains; cup products are computed by any equivariant chain map $C \to C \otimes C$ preserving the augmentation, in the degrees where $C \otimes C$ is acyclic (comparison theorem); the Euler class of an oriented plane bundle and $w_{1}$ of a line bundle are the primary obstructions to a nowhere-zero section.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(The action; proved.)} $J^{2} = -1$, $Q(J(v)) = Q(v)$, $v \cdot J(v) = 0$, and $J^{a} - 1$ is invertible for $a = 1, 2, 3$: the action on the sphere is free, and $J(v)$ is a nowhere-zero tangent field.
\item \emph{(The cell complex; proved given (G).)} $S^{2n+1}$ has a $G$-invariant cell structure with one free orbit of cells $g^{a}e_{k}$ in each dimension $0 \leq k \leq 2n+1$, and $\partial e_{2r+1} = (g - 1)e_{2r}$, $\partial e_{2r} = Ne_{2r-1}$, $N = 1 + g + g^{2} + g^{3}$. The complex is exact in degrees $0 < k < 2n+1$.
\item \emph{(Diagonal and cup products; proved given (G).)} The map $\Delta(e_{k}) = \sum_{p+q=k}\Delta_{p,q}$ with $\Delta_{p,q} = e_{p} \otimes e_{q}$ for $p$ even, $e_{p} \otimes g e_{q}$ for $p$ odd and $q$ even, and $\sum_{0 \leq r < j \leq 3} g^{r}e_{p} \otimes g^{j}e_{q}$ for $p, q$ odd, extended equivariantly for the diagonal action, is a chain map preserving the augmentation. With $\varepsilon_{k}$ the invariant cochain equal to $1$ on $e_{k}$: $\delta\varepsilon_{2r-1} = 4\varepsilon_{2r}$, $\delta\varepsilon_{2r} = 0$, and $\varepsilon_{p} \cup \varepsilon_{q} = \varepsilon_{p+q}$ unless $p$ and $q$ are both odd, when it is $6\varepsilon_{p+q}$. Hence $H^{2r}(\Sig_{n}; \Z) = \Z_{4}$ for $1 \leq r \leq n$, generated by $y^{r}$, $y := [\varepsilon_{2}]$; $H^{\mathrm{odd}}(\Sig_{n}; \Z) = 0$ below the top degree and $H^{2n+1} = \Z$; $H^{\mathrm{even}}(\Sig_{n}; \Z) = \Z[y]/(4y, y^{n+1})$. With $\Z_{2}$ coefficients every $\varepsilon_{k}$ is a cocycle, $x := [\varepsilon_{1}]$ and $u := [\varepsilon_{2}]$ generate, $x^{2} = 6u = 0$, $xu^{r} = [\varepsilon_{2r+1}] \neq 0$, so $H^{*}(\Sig_{n}; \Z_{2}) = \Lambda[x] \otimes \Z_{2}[u]/(u^{n+1})$ and $u$ is the reduction of $y$. With $\Z_{4}$ coefficients the square of the degree-one generator is $2[\varepsilon_{2}] \neq 0$. For the same formulas with $\Z_{2}$ in place of $\Z_{4}$ (real projective space) the coefficient is $1$ and $x^{2} \neq 0$.
\item \emph{(Bocksteins; proved given (G).)} The integral Bockstein of $x$ is $\beta x = 2y$, of order two. The Bockstein of $0 \to \Z_{2} \to \Z_{4} \to \Z_{2} \to 0$ vanishes on every class of $H^{*}(\Sig_{n}; \Z_{2})$, and every such class lifts to $\Z_{4}$ coefficients. Given the classical identification of $Sq^{1}$ with this Bockstein, $Sq^{1} = 0$ on $H^{*}(\Sig_{n}; \Z_{2})$.
\item \emph{(Bundles; proved given (G).)} $w_{1}(\shL) = x$; the Euler class of $\eta$ is $\pm y$ and that of $\eta^{2} = \shL \oplus \shL$ is $\pm 2y$ (the sign is the orientation convention), of orders four and two; and $T\Sig_{n} \oplus \underline{\R} \cong (n+1)\,\eta$.
\item \emph{(The K-ring; proved given (K1).)} Let (K1) be the classical facts: complex K-theory of a finite complex $X$ is a commutative ring with a multiplicative decreasing filtration $F^{2r}$ (classes vanishing on the $(2r-1)$-skeleton); when $H^{\mathrm{odd}}(X; \Z)$ is zero or torsion-free and concentrated in the top degree, $F^{2r}/F^{2r+2} \cong H^{2r}(X; \Z)$ compatibly with products; and for a line bundle $\ell$ the class $\ell - 1$ lies in $F^{2}$ with image $c_{1}(\ell)$, the Euler class of the underlying plane bundle. Then, with $\chi$ the class of $\eta$ as a complex line and $s = \chi - 1$: $\chi^{4} = 1$, $s^{n+1} = 0$, the $4^{n}$ elements $\sum_{r=1}^{n}a_{r}s^{r}$, $0 \leq a_{r} < 4$, are distinct and exhaust the reduced group, and $K(\Sig_{n}) \cong \Z[\chi]/(\chi^{4} - 1, (\chi - 1)^{n+1})$, whose augmentation ideal has order exactly $4^{n}$. In this ring the order of $1 - \chi^{2}$ is $2^{\lfloor (n+1)/2 \rfloor}$ for $1 \leq n \leq 9$ (computed); in particular $2(1 - \chi^{2}) = 0$ for $n = 1, 2$ and not for $n = 3$.
\end{enumerate}
Not derived: the spin class $q_{1}$ with $2q_{1} = p_{1}$; the lambda-operations of K-theory; (K1) itself; the background (G).

## technical
Two stored results on the rung count of lens-space walls were conditional on classical facts about the lens spaces $L^{2n+1}(4)$, cited from memory. This result derives those that can be derived at reasonable length, and says exactly which remain cited. The sphere carries a cell structure with one orbit of cells in each dimension, whose chain complex over the group ring alternates multiplication by $g - 1$ and by the norm element; it is the beginning of the standard periodic resolution of a cyclic group. An explicit equivariant diagonal on this complex, checked to be a chain map in integer arithmetic (the formulas repeat with period two in each degree, so finitely many cases cover all), gives the cup products of the quotient by counting terms: all products of the invariant cochains have coefficient one, except a product of two odd-degree cochains, which has coefficient six, the number of ordered pairs $r < j$ among four group elements. So the integral cohomology in even degrees is a truncated polynomial ring on a class of order four, the degree-one class with coefficients mod two squares to zero, and the same count for the group of order two gives coefficient one, the familiar nonzero square on projective space. The Bocksteins are read from the coboundary $4\varepsilon_{2r}$: the integral Bockstein of the degree-one class is twice the generator, and the Bockstein that represents the first Steenrod square vanishes identically. The Euler classes come from explicit sections in the algebra: a vector's first coordinate plane component, which winds once around the first circle, and the reflection $v e_{1} v$, which winds twice and changes sign under the quarter turn. The stable tangent bundle is read from the ambient space, on which the group acts linearly. For K-theory the full ring is not derived from nothing; it is shown to follow from the Atiyah-Hirzebruch filtration, a general property of K-theory, together with the cohomology ring derived here, by a count: the presented ring and the K-group both have reduced order $4^{n}$. The spin class used by the first stored result is not derived; it needs the cohomology of the classifying space of the spin group. All of this rests on the general machinery of cellular cohomology, which is stated as background.

## lay
Earlier results in this collection about how many extra directions are needed to repair a wall where the geometry changes signature relied on textbook facts about a family of spaces called lens spaces, quoted from memory. This result works those facts out inside the collection. A lens space here is a sphere in which each point is identified with its images under a quarter turn. The sphere is cut into pieces that the quarter turn permutes, one family of pieces in each dimension, and the way the pieces fit together, together with a rule for how a piece sits diagonally inside the product of the sphere with itself, determines the algebra of the space's twisting classes by counting. The count shows that the simplest twist class multiplies with itself to zero, unlike on the related space made with a half turn, and that an integer class of order four survives in every even dimension. These are the facts the earlier results used. Two further ingredients they used are not worked out here and remain quoted: a refined class of spinning bundles, and the general theory behind a finer invariant called K-theory, although the particular K-theory fact about lens spaces is reduced to that general theory.

## one-liner
From the equivariant cell structure of the sphere under the quarter turn and an explicit diagonal approximation, $H^{\mathrm{even}}(L^{2n+1}(4); \Z) = \Z[y]/(4y, y^{n+1})$, $H^{*}(L^{2n+1}(4); \Z_{2}) = \Lambda[x] \otimes \Z_{2}[u]/(u^{n+1})$ with $x^{2} = 0$, $\beta x = 2y$, the mod-2 Bockstein vanishes, the quarter-turn and half-turn plane bundles have Euler classes $\pm y$ and $\pm 2y$, $T\Sig \oplus \underline{\R} \cong (n+1)\eta$, and the K-ring $\Z[\chi]/(\chi^{4} - 1, (\chi - 1)^{n+1})$ follows from the Atiyah-Hirzebruch filtration; the spin class is not derived.

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{(1).} $B$ is a sum of commuting unit bivectors of square $-1$ in orthogonal planes, and $v \cdot B$ turns the component of $v$ in each plane by a quarter turn: $e_{1} \cdot (e_{1}e_{2}) = e_{2}$, $e_{2} \cdot (e_{1}e_{2}) = -e_{1}$. So $J$ is orthogonal with $J^{2} = -1$, $v \cdot J(v) = 0$, and $J^{a}$, $a = 1, 2, 3$, has no eigenvalue $1$. The check verifies these in $\Cl(6,0)$.

\emph{(2).} Write $\R^{2n+2} = P_{0} \oplus \dots \oplus P_{n}$ with $P_{r}$ the plane of $e_{2r+1}, e_{2r+2}$, and $S^{2r+1}$ the unit sphere of $P_{0} \oplus \dots \oplus P_{r}$. Let $e_{2r}$ be the set of $v \in S^{2r+1}$ whose $P_{r}$-component is a non-negative multiple of $e_{2r+1}$, and $e_{2r+1}$ the set of $v \in S^{2r+1}$ whose $P_{r}$-component lies in the open quarter plane between $e_{2r+1}$ and $J(e_{2r+1})$. Then $e_{2r}$ is a closed $2r$-disc with boundary $S^{2r-1}$ (it is the join of $S^{2r-1}$ with the point $e_{2r+1}$), $e_{2r+1}$ is an open $(2r+1)$-cell (the join of $S^{2r-1}$ with an open arc) whose closure adds $e_{2r}$, $g e_{2r}$ and $S^{2r-1}$, the translates $g^{a}e_{k}$ are disjoint and cover $S^{2r+1} \setminus S^{2r-1}$, and $g$ permutes them freely. With orientations chosen inductively and carried by $g$, the boundary of $e_{2r+1}$ is $g e_{2r} - e_{2r}$ (the two ends of the arc), and the boundary of $e_{2r}$ is the whole sphere $S^{2r-1}$, the sum of its four top cells $g^{a}e_{2r-1}$. On the group ring $\Z[G]$, multiplication by $g - 1$ has kernel the multiples of $N$ (an element fixed by $g$ has equal coefficients) and $N u = (\text{sum of the coefficients of } u)\,N$ has kernel the elements of coefficient sum zero, which is the image of $g - 1$. So the complex is exact in degrees $0 < k < 2n+1$, as it must be for a sphere. The check verifies $\partial^{2} = 0$ and the two ranks.

\emph{(3).} \emph{Chain map.} The formulas for $\Delta_{p,q}$ and for $\partial$ depend on $p$ and $q$ only through their parities, apart from the vanishing of $\partial$ in degree zero. So the identity $\partial\Delta(e_{k}) = \Delta(\partial e_{k})$, with $\partial(u \otimes v) = \partial u \otimes v + (-1)^{p}u \otimes \partial v$, has components indexed by $(p, q)$ with $p + q = k - 1$ that depend only on the parities of $p$ and $q$ and on whether $p$ or $q$ is zero; all these cases occur for $k \leq 5$. The check verifies the identity for $k \leq 9$ in exact integer arithmetic, for groups of order $2$, $3$ and $4$, and that $\Delta(e_{0}) = e_{0} \otimes e_{0}$. (The underlying mechanism is $\sum_{r<j} g^{r} \otimes g^{j}$ intertwining $g \otimes g - 1 \otimes 1$ with $N \otimes g - 1 \otimes N$.) By the comparison theorem of (G), since $C \otimes C$ has no homology in degrees $0 < k < 2n+1$, $\Delta$ is chain homotopic through degree $2n$ to a cellular approximation of the geometric diagonal, so it computes cup products into degrees at most $2n$. For products into the top degree $2n+1$, include $S^{2n+1}$ in $S^{2n+3}$ as the subcomplex of cells of dimension at most $2n+1$: the restriction $H^{*}(\Sig_{n+1}) \to H^{*}(\Sig_{n})$ is a ring map which on cochains sends $\varepsilon_{k}$ to $\varepsilon_{k}$ for $k \leq 2n+1$, and in $\Sig_{n+1}$ the degree $2n+1$ is below the top.

\emph{Cochains.} An invariant cochain with trivial coefficients is a multiple of $\varepsilon_{k}$ in each degree. $(\delta\varepsilon_{k-1})(e_{k}) = \varepsilon_{k-1}(\partial e_{k})$ is $1 - 1 = 0$ for $k$ odd and $4$ for $k$ even. So the integral cochain complex is $\Z$ in each degree with coboundary $0, 4, 0, 4, \dots$: $H^{2r} = \Z_{4}$ for $1 \leq r \leq n$, $H^{2r-1} = 0$ for $1 \leq r \leq n$, $H^{2n+1} = \Z$. $(\varepsilon_{p} \cup \varepsilon_{q})(e_{p+q}) = (\varepsilon_{p} \otimes \varepsilon_{q})(\Delta_{p,q})$ is the number of terms of $\Delta_{p,q}$: $1$, or $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ when both are odd. So $[\varepsilon_{2}]^{r} = [\varepsilon_{2r}]$, a generator, and $y^{n+1} = 0$ for want of cells: $H^{\mathrm{even}} = \Z[y]/(4y, y^{n+1})$. Modulo $2$ all coboundaries vanish, $x^{2} = 6[\varepsilon_{2}] = 0$, $xu^{r} = [\varepsilon_{2r+1}]$, $u^{r} = [\varepsilon_{2r}]$, which is the stated ring; modulo $4$ all coboundaries vanish too and $[\varepsilon_{1}]^{2} = 2[\varepsilon_{2}]$. The sign conventions of the cup product change none of these statements. For the group of order two the same formulas give $\binom{2}{2} = 1$.

\emph{(4).} The integral cochain $\varepsilon_{1}$ lifts the mod-$2$ cocycle representing $x$, and $\delta\varepsilon_{1} = 4\varepsilon_{2} = 2 \cdot 2\varepsilon_{2}$, so $\beta x = [2\varepsilon_{2}] = 2y$, of order two in $\Z_{4}$. For the sequence $\Z_{2} \to \Z_{4} \to \Z_{2}$: every mod-$2$ cocycle $\varepsilon_{k}$ lifts to the mod-$4$ cochain $\varepsilon_{k}$, whose coboundary is $0$ or $4\varepsilon_{k+1} \equiv 0$ modulo $4$; so the lift is a cocycle and the Bockstein is zero.

\emph{(5).} $\shL$ is the flat line with holonomy $-1$ around the loop that is the image of the path $e_{1}$ from the base point to its translate; a section over the base point extends over that loop only with a sign change, so the obstruction cocycle is $\varepsilon_{1}$ modulo $2$: $w_{1}(\shL) = x$. For $\eta$: a section is a map $\sigma$ from the sphere to the plane with $\sigma(J(v)) = J\sigma(v)$; take $\sigma_{1}(v)$ the $P_{0}$-component of $v$. It is nowhere zero on the $1$-skeleton $S^{1}$, and on the boundary of $e_{2}$, which is $S^{1}$ traversed once (the sum $Ne_{1}$), it is the identity map of the circle, of degree $1$. The obstruction cocycle is therefore $\pm\varepsilon_{2}$ and the Euler class $\pm y$. For $\eta^{2}$: $\sigma_{2}(v) = w e_{1} w$ with $w$ the $P_{0}$-component of $v$ satisfies $\sigma_{2}(J(v)) = -\sigma_{2}(v)$, is nowhere zero on $S^{1}$, and is the double-angle map there (verified in the check at rational points of the circle), of degree $2$: Euler class $\pm 2y$. Tangent bundle: at $v \in S^{2n+1}$, $\R^{2n+2} = T_{v}S^{2n+1} \oplus \R v$, and the linear map $J$ acts on this splitting equivariantly, fixing the radial section $v \mapsto v$. So $TS^{2n+1} \oplus \underline{\R}$ is the product bundle with fibre $\R^{2n+2} = P_{0} \oplus \dots \oplus P_{n}$ on which $g$ acts by the quarter turn in each plane, and dividing by $G$ gives $T\Sig_{n} \oplus \underline{\R} \cong (n+1)\eta$.

\emph{(6).} $\chi^{4}$ is the flat line with trivial holonomy, so $\chi^{4} = 1$. By (K1), $s = \chi - 1 \in F^{2}$ with image $c_{1}(\eta) = \pm y$ by (5), and by multiplicativity $s^{r} \in F^{2r}$ with image $\pm y^{r}$, a generator of $H^{2r} = \Z_{4}$ by (3); $s^{n+1} \in F^{2n+2} = 0$. By (3) the odd cohomology is zero below the top degree and $\Z$ there, so (K1) applies and the reduced group has a filtration with quotients $\Z_{4}$, $n$ times: its order is $4^{n}$. If $\sum a_{r}s^{r} = \sum b_{r}s^{r}$ with $0 \leq a_{r}, b_{r} < 4$ and $j$ the least index with $a_{j} \neq b_{j}$, the difference lies in $F^{2j}$ with image $\pm(a_{j} - b_{j})y^{j} \neq 0$, a contradiction; so these $4^{n}$ elements are distinct and are all of the reduced group. Hence the ring map $\Z[\chi]/(\chi^{4} - 1, (\chi - 1)^{n+1}) \to K(\Sig_{n})$ is onto. The augmentation ideal of the presented ring is spanned by $s, \dots, s^{n}$ with relations $s^{j}\bigl((1+s)^{4} - 1\bigr) = s^{j}(4s + 6s^{2} + 4s^{3} + s^{4})$, $0 \leq j < n$, a triangular system with diagonal entries $4$: order $4^{n}$. A surjection between finite groups of the same order is a bijection. The order of $1 - \chi^{2} = -(2s + s^{2})$ is the least $N$ with $N(2s + s^{2})$ in the relation lattice, computed exactly in the check for $n \leq 9$.
